slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: From factory floors to daily life — how human-shaped machines are reshaping our world in 2026

slides.heading: Why Human-Shaped?
slides.body: Humanoid robots are designed to operate in spaces built for people — using stairs, doorknobs, and tools humans already use. This design philosophy means they can slot into existing infrastructure without costly retrofits.

slides.heading: The Manufacturing Revolution
slides.body: Major automakers and electronics factories have deployed thousands of humanoid robots on assembly lines. They handle repetitive, physically demanding tasks and work alongside humans — boosting output without replacing entire workforces overnight.

slides.heading: Learning by Watching
slides.body: Modern humanoids learn from human demonstration. Workers perform a task once while the robot observes and records motion data. Within hours, the robot can replicate the task — dramatically cutting training time compared to traditional programming.

slides.heading: The AI Brain Inside
slides.body: Each robot is powered by large multimodal AI models that process vision, language, and touch simultaneously. This lets them interpret spoken instructions, recognize objects in clutter, and adapt grip pressure to fragile items in real time.

slides.heading: Home and Care Applications
slides.body: Pilot programs in Japan and South Korea are placing humanoid assistants in elder-care facilities. They remind residents to take medication, assist with mobility, and provide companionship — addressing a critical caregiver shortage.

slides.heading: Safety and Liability Challenges
slides.body: Robots operating near humans must fail safely. Regulators are still writing the rulebook: who is liable when a robot causes injury? Current standards require robots to detect human proximity and reduce force before contact occurs.

slides.heading: The Cost Curve Is Dropping
slides.body: In 2023 a humanoid robot cost over $200,000. By 2026 mass production has pushed prices below $30,000 — comparable to a mid-range car. Analysts project sub-$10,000 units within five years as volumes scale.

slides.heading: Ethical Questions We Must Answer
slides.body: As humanoids take on more roles, societies face hard questions: Which jobs should remain human? How do we retrain displaced workers? And how do we prevent emotional over-attachment to machines designed to seem human?

slides.heading: The Robot Decade Has Begun
slides.body: Humanoid robots are no longer science fiction — they are on factory floors, in care homes, and at our doorsteps. Staying informed and shaping policy now is the best way to ensure this technology works for everyone.
